extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners interested in the philosophy and practice of scientific method (scientists, philosophers of science, advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for forming, testing, and accepting scientific hypotheses — when a hypothesis is legitimate, how it must be tested (induction, ratiocination, verification), and what constraints (vera causa, testability, susceptibility to independent evidence) it must satisfy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition which we make (either without actual evidence, or on evidence avowedly insufficient) in order to endeavor to deduce from it conclusions in accordance with facts which are known to be real; under the idea that if the conclusions to which the hypothesis leads are known truths, the hypothesis itself either must be, or at least is likely to be, true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are invented to enable earlier use of the Deductive Method and to explain phenomena by feigning laws or causes when known laws do not suffice. They may concern causes or laws of correspondence between facts and serve primarily to suggest deductions and lines of investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part proof process (induction, ratiocination, verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover a cause by the Deductive Method the process must consist of three parts: induction (ascertain laws of the causes), ratiocination (compute consequences from those laws), and verification (compare calculated effect with the actual phenomenon). No one of these three parts can be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying deduction to establish a cause, ensure you have (or can obtain) the inductive law, perform the deduction, and then verify by comparing with observation (example: Newton's proof equating terrestrial gravity with the central force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy condition for the Hypothetical Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hypothetical Method (assuming a law and using ratiocination and verification while suppressing induction) is legitimate only if the final verification fulfills the conditions of a complete induction — i.e., if no false law could lead to the same true results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothetical assumption is permissible only when verification can functionally stand as induction, meaning the observed agreement could not arise except from the assumed law (example: Newton's deduction of the inverse-square law fulfilled this proviso because alternate laws would give inconsistent results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference requirement (positive and negative instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove identity of cause by deduction one must obtain both instances required by the Method of Difference: the affirmative instance (A B C → a b c) and the negative instance (B C → b c), showing that only the assumed antecedent produces the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your verification supplies both sorts of instance — the positive (deduced from hypothesis) and the negative (showing absence of effect without the hypothesized antecedent). These may be obtained by deduction or experiment; lacking the negative instance precludes conclusive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa (cause must be a real, detectable phenomenon)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuinely scientific hypothesis relating to causation should be of such a nature that it can be proved or disproved by comparison with observed facts; the supposed cause should be a real phenomenon, or at least capable of being detected and shown to exercise influence by independent evidence (the 'vera causa' requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the cause be known beforehand, but it must be susceptible of independent demonstration later. Hypotheses proposing causes that cannot ever be independently detected (or tested) are philosophically weak (e.g., Descartes' vortices if they could not in principle be tested).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testability / falsifiability constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis should be such that if it were false it would lead to results at variance with true facts; i.e., a false law should not be able to lead to the same true consequences as the true law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a hypothesis, check whether alternative (false) laws could produce identical observable consequences. If many distinct hypotheses could equally account for the known facts, the hypothesis lacks conclusive scientific warrant until further discriminating tests are proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to independent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis should suggest observations and experiments that can provide independent evidence for the cause it posits; its existence and its causal relation to the effect should be provable by means other than the mere fact that it explains the known phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that supply a route to independent confirmation (for instance, by predicting new, testable phenomena or by enabling detection of the postulated agent). Hypotheses that cannot be put to such independent tests should be treated as provisional conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive success increases plausibility but is not conclusive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: That a hypothesis has led to the anticipation and prediction of phenomena subsequently verified increases its plausibility, but such coincidences do not amount to conclusive proof of the hypothesis' truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use predictive confirmations as supporting evidence but remain cautious: multiple hypotheses might predict the same observations; even many coincidences would not strictly prove the real mechanism (examples: undulatory theory successes do not logically force acceptance of undulations as the true mechanism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy with known laws increases plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses which ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature possess greater plausibility than wholly arbitrary suppositions; scientists commonly posit causes resembling known agents and laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing hypotheses, favor those that align with established kinds of phenomena or laws (e.g., assuming motions similar to known undulatory laws). Nevertheless, analogy alone is not decisive and must be complemented by ability to test and by independent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional and indispensable role of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are indispensable provisional steps in scientific inquiry: they provide inducement to attempt particular experiments, guide the direction of investigation, and serve as tentative theories to be corrected by subsequent comparison with facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheses as working tools: begin with the simplest supposition consistent with data, iteratively correct it as new observations are compared with its consequences, and recognize that many current theories began as hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and tractability as virtues in initial hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest supposition which accords with the more obvious facts is the best to begin with, because its consequences are the most easily traced; start with a 'rude hypothesis' and correct it iteratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, tractable assumptions to make consequences clear and experiment design feasible. Prefer hypotheses that make deductions easier to trace so that discrepancies reveal how to refine the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hypotheses about causation from laws of correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses may concern either the cause or only the law of correspondence between accompanying facts (without asserting causation). Both types can be legitimate provided they lead to testable consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a hypothesis, be explicit whether it asserts a causal mechanism or merely a law of correlation; both can be scientifically valuable but the standards for independent demonstration differ (causal claims require showing the agent's influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of inferring unobservable agents solely from explanatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: The weak point in some accounts (e.g., vibrations of a hypothetical fluid) is that the existence and motion of the postulated medium are assumed solely because they explain phenomena; explanatory power alone is insufficient evidence for unobserved entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand additional kinds of evidence for unobserved entities (e.g., independent detection, new discriminating predictions). Do not accept a hypothesis merely because it affords a convenient explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of negative-instance demonstration when cause is novel
rubrics_metrics.description: When the cause assumed in the hypothesis is an unknown cause imagined solely to account for an effect, one cannot obtain assurance of its truth merely by deducing the known facts: it is necessary also to obtain the negative instance showing that without that cause the effect would not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for newly posited causes, design tests that demonstrate that alternative antecedents would not produce the observed effect; failing to secure such discrimination leaves the hypothesis unproven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness criterion: hypothesis should open a practical route of investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is useful if, by suggesting a line of investigation, it may terminate in obtaining real proof; it is illegitimate if it cannot lead to any course of investigation capable of converting it from an hypothesis into a proved fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize hypotheses that generate concrete experimental or observational programs leading to independent confirmation or refutation (example: Descartes' vortices were objectionable because direct tests eventually refuted them by observation of comets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic method of approximation (iterative correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific inquiry commonly proceeds by making provisional conjectures, deducing consequences, comparing them with the facts, and correcting the hypothesis repeatedly — akin to the Methods of Approximation in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an iterative approach: extemporize a first crude theory from a subset of facts, test it against remaining data, and revise; this process often leads provisional hypotheses to become established theories.
